unit.title: Perpetual review
unit.summary: Spaced retrieval of mastered concepts across the whole course.

lessons.title: Daily Bite
lessons.objective: Retrieve five due concepts in about two minutes.

payload.prompt: How many points does a Grand Prix win score?

options.text: 25 points
options.explanation: Right. A win is 25, then 18 for second and 15 for third.

options.text: 20 points
options.explanation: Not any more. The scale has been 25 for a win since 2010.

options.text: 18 points plus one for fastest lap
options.explanation: Eighteen is second place, and the fastest-lap point was dropped from 2025.

options.text: 15 points
options.explanation: Fifteen is third place. The winner gets 25.

explanation.correct: A win is worth 25 points, and the top ten score 25-18-15-12-10-8-6-4-2-1.
explanation.incorrect: A win scores 25. Second scores 18, third 15, and there is no extra point for fastest lap.

payload.prompt: Why does an undercut gain time on a rival?

options.text: The car behind stops first, gets fresh tyres, and is faster on the next lap.
options.explanation: Right. Fresh rubber beats old tyres for pace.

options.text: The pit lane is shorter if you pit early.
options.explanation: No, the pit lane does not change length mid-race.

options.text: Fresh tyres are automatically faster by a fixed amount.
options.explanation: Not automatic. Pace gain depends on how old the old tyres are.

options.text: It saves fuel, which makes the car lighter.
options.explanation: F1 has not had refuelling since 2010.

explanation.correct: Right. The first to pit gets fresh grip while rivals are on old tyres.
explanation.incorrect: An undercut works because fresh tyres are faster than worn tyres.
explanation.sayThisLine: Pit first, get fresh tyres, jump ahead when they stop.

payload.prompt: How does downforce help a race car in a corner?

options.text: It pushes the car into the track, increasing grip.
options.explanation: Right. Downforce = more grip = faster cornering.

options.text: It keeps the car from flipping over.
options.explanation: Downforce does add stability, but the main benefit is grip for speed.

options.text: It pushes the driver back in the seat for comfort.
options.explanation: Downforce affects the car's grip, not the driver's comfort.

options.text: It reduces drag so the car accelerates faster.
options.explanation: No, downforce brings drag as a side effect. Drag slows.

explanation.correct: Right. Downforce = grip = ability to go fast through corners.
explanation.incorrect: Downforce is aerodynamic force that pushes the car into the track.
explanation.sayThisLine: More downforce means the car can corner faster.

payload.template: When a safety car is deployed, it {{result}} the field by slowing everyone to the same pace.

explanation.correct: Right. The safety car bunches the pack, erasing the gaps built up in the race.
explanation.incorrect: A safety car bunches the field, closing up all the gaps between cars.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: The wings open on the straights and close for the corners. It is like a two-speed wing.

payload.question: What is she describing?

options.text: Active aero: Straight Mode for low drag and Corner Mode for grip.
options.explanation: Yes. The wings move to trade drag against downforce as the lap changes.

options.text: A pit-stop routine for changing the wings.
options.explanation: The wings move while the car is on track, not in the pits.

options.text: A mechanical failure that makes the wings flap.
options.explanation: It is a designed feature of the 2026 cars.

options.text: A penalty for running the wing too low.
options.explanation: It is not a penalty. It is how the cars work.

payload.translation: The 2026 cars have moving wings. On straights they go to low drag, and for braking and corners they return to the high-downforce setting.

followUps.line: Is the switch manual or automatic?
followUps.why: A genuine question about how active aero is controlled.
DRS only opened one flap for a chasing car. Active aero is for everyone.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you are not sure about the details, ask how the switching works.

lessons.title: Weekend recap review
lessons.objective: Refresh the concepts that appeared in the latest race.

payload.prompt: Why is a pit stop under a safety car called 'cheap'?

options.text: Because the pit crew is paid less under a safety car.
options.explanation: No, the crew is the same. The pit lane cost is lower.

options.text: Because the cost in time is much smaller than a normal stop.
options.explanation: Right. The field is slow, so stopping costs less lap time.

options.text: Because no tyres are changed during a safety car.
options.explanation: No, teams do change tyres; the pit lane is just slower.

options.text: Because the team does not have to pay for fuel.
options.explanation: F1 has not had refuelling since 2010. Wrong era.

explanation.correct: Right. Under a safety car, the whole field is slowed, so pit-lane time loss is small.
explanation.incorrect: A cheap stop under a safety car costs less time because the field is slow.
explanation.sayThisLine: Under the safety car, the pit stop is cheap.

payload.prompt: What does tyre degradation mean in a Grand Prix?

options.text: The tyre loses grip and lap time as the stint goes on.
options.explanation: Right. Tyre wear is the main variable in race strategy.

options.text: The tyre completely fails and forces a DNF.
options.explanation: Degradation is slow loss of grip, not sudden failure.

options.text: The tyre pressure drops because of the heat.
options.explanation: Pressure is monitored and managed; deg is the grip loss.

options.text: The tyre looks discoloured after the race.
options.explanation: Colour change does not define degradation. It is lap-time loss.

explanation.correct: Right. Tyres get slower lap by lap. Managing this is strategy.
explanation.incorrect: Degradation is the gradual loss of grip and speed as tyres age.
explanation.sayThisLine: His fronts are degrading; pace has dropped.

payload.prompt: What does a five-second time penalty mean in a race?

options.text: Five seconds is added to the driver's race time, often served at a pit stop.
options.explanation: Right. The driver's finishing order is worked out after the time is added.

options.text: The driver starts five places lower at the next race.
options.explanation: That is a grid penalty, which is a different thing.

options.text: The whole race is paused for five seconds.
options.explanation: Only the penalised driver is affected.

options.text: The driver loses five championship points.
options.explanation: Time penalties change the order, not the points directly.

explanation.correct: Five seconds added to the finishing time can drop a driver several places if the gaps behind are small.
explanation.incorrect: A time penalty adds seconds to a driver's race time. The classification is worked out with the extra time included.
explanation.sayThisLine: Five seconds could cost him two places.

payload.template: If tyres {{condition}} too quickly, the team must pit earlier than planned.

explanation.correct: Right. Fast degradation forces an early stop to avoid the tyre cliff.
explanation.incorrect: If tyres degrade too fast, the team has to pit earlier than planned.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: Ten seconds for that? He only barely touched him. That is so harsh.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: She thinks a ten-second penalty is too steep for light contact.
options.explanation: Yes. She believes the penalty does not fit the incident.

options.text: The stewards gave the wrong driver a penalty.
options.explanation: She is not questioning who got penalised, but the amount.

options.text: She wants a grid penalty instead of a time penalty.
options.explanation: Not mentioned. She is about the size of the penalty.

options.text: The penalty was applied at the wrong time.
options.explanation: Timing is not her concern; it is the severity.

payload.translation: She thinks the stewards gave a too-harsh time penalty for a minor collision.

followUps.line: What penalty would you have given for that kind of contact?
followUps.why: Asks her opinion rather than correcting; stewards' calls are always debated.

followUps.line: Did it change the race result for him?
followUps.why: Focuses on the consequence rather than the rule.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Penalty consistency is the top fan debate; there is no single 'right' call.

lessons.title: Term retrieval mix
lessons.objective: Match and complete terms from every layer, weakest first.

pairs.definition: A team that builds and races its own car.
The turbocharged engine plus electrical systems driving the car.
Works team makes its engine; customer team buys power from another.

distractorDefinitions: The fuel that powers F1 cars.

explanation.summary: Constructor builds the car; power unit is the engine. Works = own engine.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ferrari is a constructor with its own power unit.

pairs.definition: The range of laps in which a pit stop makes strategic sense.
Drafting behind a car ahead to cut drag and gain speed.
The turbulent wake that steals grip from the following car.

explanation.summary: Pit window is when to stop, the slipstream is the tow gain, and dirty air is the price of following closely.
explanation.sayThisLine: The pit window is closing, and the slipstream is hard to find in dirty air.

payload.template: The {{award}} Championship is won by the team that scores the most points across both drivers.

explanation.correct: Right. The Constructors' Championship adds both drivers' points. The Drivers' Championship is individual.
explanation.incorrect: It is the Constructors' Championship for teams. The Drivers' Championship is for individuals.

payload.template: The {{effect}} behind a car ahead lets the following driver cut drag on the straight.

explanation.correct: Right. The slipstream, or tow, cuts drag and lets the car behind gain speed down the straight.
explanation.incorrect: The slipstream, also called the tow, is what reduces drag for the car behind.

payload.prompt: What does it mean if a pit window is 'open'?

options.text: Now is a good time to pit based on tyre life and track position.
options.explanation: Right. The window is the laps where a stop makes tactical sense.

options.text: The pit lane has no traffic.
options.explanation: No, traffic can vary. The window is about timing in the race.

options.text: The team has no pit crew available.
options.explanation: Wrong. An open window means conditions are right to pit.

options.text: A safety car has just deployed.
options.explanation: Safety cars change pit timing but do not define the window.

explanation.correct: Right. When the pit window is open, stopping gains you places or position.
explanation.incorrect: A pit window is the range of laps where a pit stop makes strategic sense.
explanation.sayThisLine: The pit window is open; time to pit.

payload.prompt: When is the slipstream most useful in a race?

options.text: On long straights where the tow lets you catch up and overtake.
options.explanation: Right. The slipstream gives extra speed on the straight.

options.text: In tight corners where drafting tightens your line.
options.explanation: No, the tow is a straight-line effect. Corners lose the benefit.

options.text: During a pit stop when the car is slow.
options.explanation: The pit stop is not where you use aerodynamic effects.

options.text: Under a safety car when the field is bunched.
options.explanation: Bunching does not create more slipstream benefit than a normal race.

explanation.correct: Right. The tow on a straight is the classic overtaking setup.
explanation.incorrect: The slipstream works on straights where drag is the limiting factor.
explanation.sayThisLine: He got a tow down the back straight and pulled off an overtake.

lessons.title: Say-this refresher
lessons.objective: Decode fan lines you have already met, in new wording.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: He is within a second at the detection point. Overtake Mode is on!

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: He is close enough to get an electrical boost to attack the car ahead.
options.explanation: Yes. Within one second at the detection point makes him eligible for Overtake Mode.

options.text: He is close enough to use the DRS flap.
options.explanation: DRS ended in 2025. Overtake Mode replaced it in 2026.

options.text: He is about to pit under a safety car.
options.explanation: She is talking about a passing attempt, not a pit stop.

options.text: He has one lap left before he gets penalty points.
options.explanation: It has nothing to do with penalties.

payload.translation: He is close enough to the car ahead at the detection point to get extra electrical power, which should help him attack on the straight.

followUps.line: Does Overtake Mode guarantee a pass?
followUps.why: It does not. Dirty air and timing matter as well.

followUps.line: How is that different from DRS?
followUps.why: A natural follow-up that shows you know what changed.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Overtake Mode is a boost, not a guarantee. Ask if he made the pass.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: His best lap was deleted. Four wheels over the line at turn three on his flying lap.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: His qualifying or practice lap was cancelled for exceeding track limits.
options.explanation: Yes. Going outside the white lines voids the lap time.

options.text: He crashed and his car had to be repaired.
options.explanation: Deleted laps are about rules, not crashes.

options.text: A technical issue made the data invalid.
options.explanation: Track limits are rule-based, not technical failures.

options.text: The stewards gave him a time penalty instead.
options.explanation: Lap deletion is the track-limits consequence; no extra penalty needed.

payload.translation: His fastest qualifying or practice lap was cancelled because he drove outside the white line boundaries of the track.

followUps.line: Is he allowed to use the kerbs?
followUps.why: Asks about the boundary definition; kerbs are usually OK.

followUps.line: Can he appeal a deleted lap?
followUps.why: Shows interest in the consequence rather than judgment.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Track limits are marked by white lines; kerbs are usually fair game.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: That stint was 28 laps on softs. No way the tyres last that long. He will pit soon.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: She thinks the driver will need to pit within the next few laps because soft tyres cannot last 28 laps.
options.explanation: Yes. She is predicting tyre degradation will force a stop.

options.text: The pit stop is mandatory every 28 laps.
options.explanation: There is no fixed lap rule for stops; it is strategy and tyre life.

options.text: Soft tyres are not allowed in races.
options.explanation: Softs are allowed and often used; they just wear faster.

options.text: The team will add fuel during the stop.
options.explanation: F1 has not refuelled since 2010.

payload.translation: She is saying the driver has been on soft tyres for 28 laps, which is unsustainable due to tyre wear, so he will need to pit soon for fresh tyres.

followUps.line: Why would they choose soft tyres if they degrade so fast?
followUps.why: Asks about the trade-off: softs are quick but short-lived.

followUps.line: Could he be saving them for a later push?
followUps.why: Shows strategic thinking about tyre pacing.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Soft tyres are fast but have short life; managing this trade-off is the race.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: He hit the boost button too early on the straight and wasted it before the braking zone where he could have passed.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: He used his limited boost at the wrong moment for a passing attempt.
options.explanation: Yes. Boost is a driver button that is limited in how often it can be used, so timing matters.

options.text: He pitted at the wrong time.
options.explanation: She is talking about the boost button, not a pit stop.

options.text: He left his wings open in the braking zone.
options.explanation: Boost is electrical deployment, not a wing mode.

options.text: He got a penalty for pressing the button.
options.explanation: Using boost is allowed. Bad timing is just poor strategy.

payload.translation: He pushed the boost button too soon, so the extra electrical power was spent before the place where it would have helped him pass.

followUps.why: It is limited in how much and how often a driver can use it, so each use counts.

followUps.line: Could the engineer have told him when?
followUps.why: Teams give advice over the radio, so it is a fair question about teamwork.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Boost timing is a skill. If you are unsure, ask what he should have waited for.

payload.title: Stint strategy chat
payload.setting: Talking about the race strategy after qualifying.

exchanges.theirMessage: I think they will go for a long first stint on the hards. Three-stop race, maybe.

replies.text: Three stops is aggressive. Do you think the hard tyres can make it 25 laps?
replies.theirResponse: If they nurse them, yeah. They are trying to undercut the guys on softs.
replies.coachNote: You asked a specific question about tyre life, showing you understand stint length.

replies.theirResponse: It really is. Lots to think about.
replies.coachNote: Not wrong, but generic. Ask about their reasoning.

replies.text: Three stops seems like a waste. They should just go for the one-stop like everyone else.
replies.theirResponse: Not everyone goes one-stop. Track temps, degradation, the field changes the call.
replies.coachNote: Oversimplifying strategy. Each race has different rules and conditions.

payload.closingNote: A stint is a stretch of laps on one set of tyres; strategy is about when to stop.
